headline: The Indian Economy in an Ever More Volatile and Complex World - Special Address by Dr. Poonam Gupta, Deputy Governor, Reserve Bank of India at the 13<sup>th</sup> SBI Banking & Economics Conclave on September 23, 2026 -
summary: It is my pleasure to be here at the SBI’s 13 th Banking and Economics conclave to share my views on the Indian economy and put them in the global context-- a context that is becoming increasingly more volatile and complex. In my brief comments, I will discuss the challenges that the global economic backdrop has posed for all emerging markets including India, how the Indian policymakers have addressed these challenges to both alleviate immediate pain and turn them into opportunities, and what the near future may look like for us. I. The Global Context 2. The global economic context has become less conducive since the global financial crisis of 2008-09. Several structural shifts have impacted the growth and policy outlook for emerging market economies, including peaking of global trade, ageing societies, climate risks, and stretched public finances. While the COVID crisis of 2020-21 added an unprecedented layer of shock and complexity to the global backdrop, a fresh wave of shocks since 2022, has further aggravated it. These recent shocks include two back-to-back commodity and energy shocks amidst unending geopolitical conflicts, policy uncertainty and tariff-led disruptions in trade; an El Niño event; tech-related developments and disruptions - led by AI. 3. India has perhaps been among the most challenged emerging market economies over past year and a half. Whereas most other countries were subject to only a subset of these shocks, India has been subjected to each one of these shocks –simultaneously and cumulatively. On trade, it had faced among the highest tariffs rates the US had imposed on any partner country and an acute policy uncertainty. headline: Growth with Responsibility: The Next Balance Sheet - Special Address by Shri Swaminathan J, Deputy Governor, Reserve Bank of India at the FE Modern BFSI Summit 2026 in Mumbai on October 15, 2026 -
summary: Shri Tuhin Kanta Pandey, Chairman, SEBI; Shri Shyamal Majumdar, Editor, and friends from the Financial Express, distinguished leaders from banking, financial services and insurance; ladies and gentlemen. Good morning to all of you. 2. We meet as the festive season gathers momentum across the country— a period traditionally associated with celebration and elevated economic activity. Veterans amongst us here will recall that this was once known as the “busy season” for credit policy. For households and businesses, this is also a time when important financial decisions are often made, whether to spend or invest for the future, like purchase a home or expand an enterprise. 3. For the financial sector, this represents both opportunity and responsibility. Finance helps translate confidence into economic activity, but its ability to do so depends in turn on the confidence that customers place in financial institutions. 4. That makes the theme of today's Summit — “The Next Balance Sheet: Growth. Trust. Resilience.” — particularly relevant. The Indian financial system enters its next phase from a position of strength, with improved asset quality and comfortable capital positions. The challenge is to preserve these strengths as the system grows, becomes increasingly technology-intensive and ever more interconnected. 5. In this context, I would like to make three propositions: (i) First, as institutions pursue growth and remove friction, controls must evolve with the process. (ii) Second, trust must be treated as an asset that requires continuous investment. (iii) And third, resilience must increasingly be understood not only in terms of buffers, but also in terms of the speed with which an institution can detect, decide and recover. headline: Preserving Financial Stability in an Evolving World - Special Address by Shri Sanjay Malhotra, Governor, Reserve Bank of India, at the Fifth Kautilya Economic Conclave on October 3, 2026 -
summary: Thank you for inviting me to speak today. 2. I would like to speak on financial stability, the institutional mechanism, approach and tools for financial stability in our country, the emerging global risks, and our assessment of the financial system. I. What is Financial Stability? 3. As we all know, financial stability is the ability of the financial system to facilitate and enhance economic and financial transactions, manage risks, and absorb shocks 1 . A stable financial system is one in which financial intermediaries, markets and market infrastructures reliably provide the financial services that households and businesses depend on, including during periods of economic and financial market stress. It is a system in which households and businesses have the ability and confidence to save, borrow, invest, insure, make payments, manage risk and plan for the future 2 . II. Why financial stability? 4. One may ask the question: why talk about financial stability when the global financial system, despite repeated shocks, has been rather resilient and financial markets orderly. India too has had a stable financial system and among the strongest balance-sheets – of banks, corporates, governments and households – for a long period of time. 5. In fact, it is these very prolonged periods of stability that can encourage risk-taking and leverage, while fading memories of past crises can weaken the appetite for prudence, as Minsky's Financial Instability Hypothesis 3 reminds us. 6. I say this not because we see signs of any imminent stress but because we need to remind ourselves to remain alert to the risks. headline: Economic Resilience, Thinner Buffers, Emerging Risks Globally: Where Does India Stand?<sup>[1]</sup> - Address by Dr. Poonam Gupta, Deputy Governor, Reserve Bank of India, at the Business Standard BFSI Insight Summit -
summary: It is a pleasure to be back at the Business Standard BFSI Insight Summit. When I spoke here last year, my theme was the macroeconomic resilience of emerging markets (EMs), including India, which I attributed to the sound policy frameworks that these economies have adopted and adhered to. A year on, the resilience of the world economy has held. In today’s talk, I will reflect on the latest global outlook drawing on the recent publications of the IMF, how India is placed in this global context, and what policy priorities may be warranted for other EMs as well as India at this point in time. My observations are in four parts, one each on growth, inflation, public finances and the financial sector. 1. Growth rates seem resilient across countries The IMF’s latest World Economic Outlook (WEO, October 2026) projects the global economy to grow at 3.1 per cent in 2026 and 3.4 per cent in 2027. The projection for 2026 is 0.1 percentage point higher than in July, and that for 2027 is unchanged. While these numbers are below the pre-pandemic (2000–19) average of 3.7 per cent and the 2022–25 average of 3.5 per cent, they show continued resilience, given the underlying challenges the global economy has been facing. 2 In fact, actual growth has turned out stronger than projected by the IMF in each of the past three years, even as shocks have accumulated and intensified. A few more features of the latest projection deserve attention. First, the latest upgrade is accounted for by advanced economies (AEs), whose growth projection for 2026 has been raised by 0.4 percentage point to 2.1 per cent.
